items.prompt: If I delete the access key, how does the code on the instance get permission to read the bucket?
items.ten_second: Give the instance an IAM role. AWS hands the code short-lived credentials through the instance, so no key is stored anywhere.
sixty_second: The short answer is: you give the instance an IAM role instead of a key.
It works like this. A role has no password and no long-term keys.
You attach the role to the worker's instance through an instance profile.
AWS then delivers temporary credentials for that role to the instance.
The SDK in your code finds them on its own, and AWS refreshes them automatically.
Every request is still checked against the role's permissions policy.
The thing to watch is the policy itself.
Give the worker only the bucket and the actions it needs.
In your case, I'd create one role for the worker first, then delete the root key.
Which other services does the worker call, besides Amazon S3 and Transcribe?

follow_ups.question: Do we have to rotate those credentials ourselves?
follow_ups.answer: No. Role credentials on EC2 are temporary and updated automatically. The maximum session setting of the role does not limit them on EC2.

follow_ups.question: What if one of those credentials leaks?
follow_ups.answer: Temporary credentials cannot be revoked one by one, but their permissions are evaluated each time a request is made. You revoke the role's active sessions.

items.prompt: Bucket policy or cross-account role: how should a job in one AWS account read a bucket in another account?
items.persona: a startup founder in office hours
items.ten_second: Both work. A bucket policy keeps the job in its own account. A role moves it into the other account. Both accounts must allow it.
sixty_second: Both give the job access to the other account's bucket.
The difference is whose permissions the job uses during the read.
It works like this. With a bucket policy, the job stays in its own account.
The bucket policy names the job's role, and the role's own policy allows the read.
AWS checks both accounts, and both have to say yes.
With a role, the job assumes a role in the other account.
Then it has that role's permissions only, not its own.
The thing to watch is a KMS key: the key policy has to allow the job.
In your case, the job copies files into its own bucket.
It needs both buckets at once, so I'd use the bucket policy.
Is the source data encrypted with a KMS key?
skeleton: KMS key needs its own allow

key_points.point: Across accounts AWS allows the request only if both evaluations return Allow: the caller's policy and the bucket policy.
accept: both accounts have to say yes
the role needs its own allow too

key_points.point: With a resource-based policy the caller does not give up its permissions.
accept: the job stays in its own account
the job keeps its own permissions

key_points.point: A principal that assumes a role gives up its own permissions during the session; they are not cumulative.
accept: the job has only the role's permissions
it swaps its permissions

key_points.point: Amazon EC2 does not support resource-based policies, so access to EC2 in another account uses a role.
accept: EC2 needs a role
no policy on an instance

key_points.point: With a KMS key, the key policy and the caller's IAM policy both have to allow the use.
accept: the key needs its own permission

must_not_say.error: the bucket policy alone is enough across accounts
must_not_say.correct: Across accounts AWS allows the request only if both evaluations return Allow.

must_not_say.error: after it assumes the role, the job keeps its own permissions too
must_not_say.correct: The permissions are not cumulative. During the role session the job has the role's permissions only.

follow_ups.question: Can we name the analysts group in the bucket policy?
follow_ups.answer: No. You cannot identify a user group as a principal. Name a role of that account instead.

follow_ups.question: If we add their account to the role's trust policy, are we done?
follow_ups.answer: No. That is only half of the cross-account trust. Their side also allows sts:AssumeRole on the role ARN.

items.prompt: What is the difference between a service control policy and a permissions boundary?
items.ten_second: Both are ceilings and grant nothing. An SCP limits whole accounts in an organization. A boundary limits one user or one role.
sixty_second: Both are ceilings, and neither one grants a permission.
The difference is who they cover.
It works like this. An SCP is attached to an account or an organizational unit.
It limits every user and role in those member accounts, even the root user.
A permissions boundary is attached to one user or one role.
It limits what the policies of that identity can ever allow.
In both cases, an identity-based or resource-based policy still has to grant the action.
The thing to watch is the management account: SCPs don't apply there.
In your case, use a boundary when developers create roles for their own apps.
Add SCPs later, when you split into several accounts.
Do your developers create IAM roles themselves today?

follow_ups.question: Does an SCP limit our management account too?
follow_ups.answer: No. SCPs do not affect users or roles in the management account, so keep workloads out of it.

follow_ups.question: If the boundary allows Amazon S3, can the developer read the bucket?
follow_ups.answer: Only when a policy grants the read: an identity-based policy, or in one account a resource-based policy. The boundary sets the maximum and does not grant permissions.
